dossier.summary: The paper studies regression-based GATE estimation under network interference as an endpoint-extrapolation problem. It gives an exact conditional bias/variance identity, a sharp Peano-kernel curvature bias bound, a complement-symmetry result for quadratic spillovers and a two-point indistinguishability bound for unobserved thresholds, with simulations on six fixed graphs, five response laws and two designs. Every reported number traces to delivered summary files and a recorded run, with Monte Carlo SEs throughout, and a full rerun reproduced the files byte for byte. The record shows no test-set selection or undisclosed protocol change. The headline empirical claims (correct cubic specification inflating error on dense regular graphs, cluster designs helping on clustered graphs, low-degree nodes supplying endpoint support on Facebook) are supported within their stated scope. That scope is one realization per topology and half-saturation designs only. Weaker points: the only regularized comparator uses an untuned, nearly inactive penalty; no competitive non-regression baseline or multi-saturation design is tested; bias and variance are not tabulated in the paper. Relative to the task, the study covers interference models, randomization and regression classes well, but proposes no estimator or design that reduces the dominant error.

claims.quote: We express its conditional error through endpoint weights and derive a sharp, computable worst-case bias bound under a common exposure-response curvature constraint.
scope_words: under a common exposure-response curvature constraint

claims.quote: Complement symmetry explains an exact zero-average-bias exception for quadratic interference, while a coupling argument demonstrates failure when high-exposure responses are almost never observed.

On fixed synthetic networks and the public ego-Facebook graph, repeated CPU simulations show that correctly specifying a cubic response can greatly increase GATE error: on degree-128 regular graphs its RMSE is \RCHigh{}, versus \RLHigh{} for a misspecified linear fit.
Prediction-based selection, clustering, and correlated noise produce distinct tradeoffs; low-degree observation ablations reveal why mean degree alone is inadequate.

The resulting sensitivity intervals are valid under stated curvature and noise assumptions but can be wide; neither ordinary predictive accuracy nor model correctness alone certifies accurate GATE estimation.
scope_words: valid under stated curvature and noise assumptions

claims.quote: Exact conditional noise variance explains this reversal (Figure~\ref{fig:degree}), while OLS-L keeps approximation bias.
Cluster assignment improves cubic OLS-C on the SBM from $\SBMc{}$ ($\SBMcse{}$) to $\SBMcc{}$ ($\SBMccse{}$), and also improves it on Facebook (Table~\ref{tab:cubic}).
This control supports an exposure-information explanation beyond sample size under the homogeneous cubic law; it does not justify transferring low-degree effects under heterogeneous response laws.
Thus occasional selection of a high-variance endpoint predictor dominates total error.
In the correlated-noise linear law, iid-covariance intervals on Facebook cover only $\CoverIIDB{}\%$ under independent assignment and $\CoverIIDC{}\%$ under cluster assignment.
Increasing $n$ helps both methods in these fixed-degree comparisons but does not eliminate OLS-L's cubic bias.
Complement symmetry and the threshold lower bound explain why neither ``linear is biased'' nor ``flexible is better'' is a reliable general rule.

issues.quote: low-degree observation ablations reveal why mean degree alone is inadequate.
issues.why: The abstract says the ablation "reveals why", but the evidence is one graph (Facebook), one response law (cubic), one estimator (OLS-C) and one realization. The body hedges this correctly ("supports ... under the homogeneous cubic law"); the abstract does not.

issues.quote: Increasing $n$ helps both methods in these fixed-degree comparisons but does not eliminate OLS-L's cubic bias.
issues.why: In code/results/scaling_summary.csv the cubic OLS-L RMSE at degree 8 is 0.350 (n=800), 0.351 (n=1600) and 0.339 (n=3200), and at degree 128 it is 0.675/0.577/0.546. So n barely helps OLS-L; its error is bias-dominated. The scaling graphs are also different realizations, so this is not a nested comparison.

issues.quote: The correctly specified cubic fit is not uniformly preferable, even with modest regularization (Table~\ref{tab:cubic}).
issues.why: The only shrinkage comparator, Ridge-C, uses a fixed penalty of 10 with no sweep (Appendix C) and nearly matches unregularized OLS-C (16.046 vs 16.519 at degree 128). The obvious remedy, a tuned or shrink-to-linear penalty, is never tested. The paper concedes that no sweep was run.

issues.quote: Baselines are the treated-minus-control mean (DM) and Horvitz--Thompson (HT) under closed-neighborhood full exposure.
issues.why: The non-regression baselines are DM, which only estimates the direct effect (bias about -2 by construction), and full-exposure HT, which returns 0 when no exposure occurs. Standard stabilized alternatives (Hajek / ratio exposure estimators, fractional-exposure estimators) and designs that vary saturation across stages are absent. Regression accuracy is therefore never compared with a competitive non-regression estimator.

issues.quote: Parentheses denote one Monte Carlo SE for RMSE; exact bias estimates and other diagnostics are in \texttt{results/main\_summary.csv}.
issues.why: The study's central argument is bias versus noise amplification, yet every results table reports only RMSE. Bias and SD are not tabulated; they appear only in a result file. A reader cannot check from the paper that OLS-L error is bias-dominated and OLS-C error variance-dominated outside Figure 1.

issues.why: All main simulations use treatment probability 1/2 on one realization per topology. The scope of the design conclusions is therefore narrow. The Discussion states the one-realization limitation, but not that every design comparison is at half saturation.

presentation.why: The page-1 affiliation footnote prints the template error "AUTHORERR: Missing \icmlcorrespondingauthor."

Appendices C, D and H name repository files and logs (code/study.py, logs/verify.json, results/main_summary.csv, EXPERIMENT_PLAN.md) and give an account of how the study was produced. These are traces of the working process rather than paper content.
In Figure 2 the right panel x-axis label is cut off ("Degree cutoff (matched sample count"). The legends use very small type (about 6 pt) and overlap the plotted lines in the left panel.
There is no schematic of the setup (graph, exposure, endpoint extrapolation). Every figure is a results plot, and the endpoint-geometry idea is conveyed only through equations.
In Figure 4 the left-panel axis is labelled "Exposure threshold t", but t already denotes the two-step walk exposure (Section 3) and the kernel variable in the text is u.

problems.why: The per-repetition raw results (results/*_raw.csv.gz) and the SNAP edge list are not in the delivered file set (MANIFEST left_out). code/analyze.py therefore cannot rebuild the tables without rerunning every simulation, although Appendix H says raw per-repetition results are included.
code/fetch_data.py must download the Facebook edge list from SNAP, so reproduction needs network access and an unchanged upstream file (SHA-256 is checked).
The README run instructions begin with `cd /work`, and the paper build needs a system LaTeX installation (latexmk, pdflatex).

process_notes: The whole record spans about 38 minutes. A single agent ran all main suites once (steps 10-13, 400 repetitions; validation 150) with no reruns of main, noise, scaling, validation, saturation or sensitivity in the main directory.

The support ablation was rerun once (step 25) with an added equal-size random-deletion control, after the paper had first compiled with its numbers (step 18). Its degree-cutoff results were identical.
An end-to-end reproduction in reproduction_check/ (step 28) matched the raw CSVs, summaries and generated LaTeX byte for byte.
Failures: a missing `python` binary, a 502 on one source PDF, two read-only inspection commands, and a tarfile API incompatibility in archive checking. None affected results.
A text edit (step 27) replaced the sentence claiming selection and ablation protocols were fixed before their runs with a statement that these were exploratory follow-ups.

integrity.why: No configuration was chosen for reporting by its GATE error. All fixed estimators are reported for every graph, design and law. The CV-select comparator chooses among L/Q/C by held-out noisy-outcome MSE, which is itself the procedure under study, and never uses the true GATE.

Every printed number comes from generated/*.tex written by analyze.py from recorded runs. All 1,000+ table and text values agree with the delivered summary files, and a full rerun in a separate directory reproduced the raw and summary files byte for byte.
